# Amélie: The Relatives Dossier

*Generated from `src/data/sisterProjects.ts` with `npm run export:verwandte`. Do not edit by hand. As of 1 Oct 2026. The same content is in the front end under Research, tab "Relatives". Short version: `amelie-relatives.md`.*

## Stance when in contact

- Kin are neither recipients nor customers. Contact is at most one short greeting with a link, no ask, no follow-up (rule 3).
- Read their FAQ and community first. Precious Plastic does not answer emails whose question is already answered there.
- When a tin is involved, always give the deep link `https://felixinberlin.github.io/Amelie/#dose=<id>`, never the home page (rule 5).
- Verify addresses from search snippets on the primary page before any sending. Nothing has been sent yet; who writes to whom is Félix’s call.

## Five lessons from the kinship

1. **The ending is part of the method.** F.A.T. Lab closed on 1 August 2015, saying its tactics no longer kept pace with control measures. The archive stayed online and a decade later a reboot followed. This supports the stop rule in `amelie-loop.md`.
2. **Executable beats listed.** Precious Plastic, WikiHouse, L’Atelier Paysan and Farm Hack give plans that get built, and survive. Bare idea lists (open-source-ideas: only 11 projects in the hall of fame against over 200 ideas) fall behind. That is Amélie’s rule 4.
3. **Idea banks fail on provenance.** According to Wikipedia, it cannot be proven that a submitted idea is original, which deters users and companies. Defensive publication (TDCommons, Zenodo) solves exactly that: dated, findable prior art.
4. **Licences are rarely CC0.** Precious Plastic, WikiHouse and L’Atelier Paysan use Creative Commons licences with share-alike or attribution, captn3m0 uses CC BY. Only F.A.T. Lab gives into the public domain. That raises follow-up questions for funders who require OSI licences.
5. **Graveyards have kin.** The Civic Tech Field Guide keeps a "graveyard" of failed civic-tech projects and a text "Learning from the civic tech graveyard". Amélie’s `08-friedhof/` is the same principle for ideas and can place itself there.

## Closest kin

*Gift, public domain, deliberate ending: the stance closest to Amélie’s.*

### F.A.T. Lab (Free Art and Technology Lab)

**Status:** ended, restarted 2025 · **Place:** international, Archiv fffff.at · **Since:** 2007

> Public-domain collective, loudly signed, productive for eight years, then deliberately ended.

**What they do.** Founded in 2007 by Evan Roth and James Powderly as a collective of artists, engineers, scientists, lawyers and musicians, "dedicated to the merging of popular culture with open source technology". Members sat in San Francisco, Mexico City, New York, Paris, London, Berlin, Amsterdam and Tokyo, many tied to the Eyebeam Art and Technology Center in New York. Examples: QR Hobo Code (2011), WifiTagger (2012), the book "The F.A.T. Manual" with over 100 projects. Nominated for the Transmediale award 2010, shown at MoMA and the New Museum. Motto: "Release early, often and with rap music."

**Model, licence, scale.** Everything published is public domain: "You may enjoy, use, modify, snipe about and republish all F.A.T. media and technologies as you see fit." Ended on 1 August 2015; Evan Roth said the web had changed, the adversaries had grown powerful and the methods outdated. The archive fffff.at stayed online, unmaintained. 2025 restart as "Free Art & Intelligence" at fffff.ai (© FOFO 2025) after "3700+ days" of silence, with posts by Dan Moore and Tobias Leingruber and the 2013 manual as a free PDF.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Nearest kin per the landscape document: radically free, loudly signed, highly productive, with a clear end. Difference: F.A.T. Lab is art and critique, Amélie delivers usable tools to named recipients. The 2025 reboot is about art and AI, exactly Amélie’s interface.

**What Amélie learns.** A project may end, and the archive can reconnect years later. Template for the stop rule and for honest archiving.

**Stance when in contact: Greeting with link.** A greeting to the reboot authors (Dan Moore, Tobias Leingruber), if at all; via the website, no ask. No contact address was visible in the text read on fffff.ai, but there is a newsletter and project pages.

**Contact routes**

- <https://fffff.at>: Archive (unmaintained, contact via website, IRC) (page read)
- <https://fffff.ai>: Reboot 2025: Free Art & Intelligence (newsletter, projects) (page read)
- <https://fffff.at/the-fat-manual/>: The F.A.T. Manual (free PDF) (snippet only, verify)

*Evidence: page read, checked 2026-10-01.*

### Aram Bartholl

**Status:** active · **Place:** Berlin / Hamburg · **Since:** 1972 geboren

> Berlin conceptual artist, F.A.T. Lab member 2009 to 2015, professor at HAW Hamburg.

**What they do.** Born in 1972 in Bremen, architecture engineer from the Berlin University of the Arts (2001). Works on the relation of the digital and the physical, anonymity and privacy. Known for "Dead Drops" (since 2010), a peer-to-peer file network of USB sticks embedded in walls, grown from five sites in New York to over 1,400 worldwide; "Map" (2006), physical replicas of the Google Maps pin at city centres; "Keepalive", a permanent installation in Lower Saxony. Visiting professorships in Kassel and at UCLA; since 2019 professor of art with digital media at HAW Hamburg. Lives and works in Berlin.

**Model, licence, scale.** Individual artist with an open, distributed practice; projects like Dead Drops work because others rebuild them without asking.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** The local face of the kinship: in Berlin, open to rebuilding, without central administration. Difference: Bartholl stays in the art world, Amélie addresses specialists.

**What Amélie learns.** A distributed work needs no operation, only a reproducible instruction that strangers carry out.

**Stance when in contact: Greeting with link.** Personal greeting if Félix wants it; via "Inquiries" on the info page. The email address sits behind a link and was not in the text read, please fetch it in the browser.

**Contact routes**

- <https://arambartholl.com/info/>: Info page with "Inquiries" (address obscured) (page read)
- <https://arambartholl.com/press/>: Press (snippet only, verify)

### Precious Plastic

**Status:** active · **Place:** Eindhoven / weltweit · **Since:** 2013

> Open plans for recycling machines, built worldwide: the executable gift.

**What they do.** Dave Hakkens started the project in 2013 while studying at Design Academy Eindhoven. Machines that grind, melt and inject plastic waste, plans and tools public. Version 4.0 (January 2020) brought business models and starter kits; the "Bazar" (since 2016) sells machines and products. In 2018 the project won the €300,000 Famae award. Since December 2020 it belongs to the umbrella One Army (with Project Kamp, PhoneBloks, Fixing Fashion, Story Hopper); "Verified" workshops followed in 2021. According to Wikipedia over 40,000 participants and over 400 workshops (check the date of the source). In 2019 Hakkens and collaborators disagreed about burning versus recycling ocean plastic.

**Model, licence, scale.** Everything under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 (not CC0). A foundation with limited resources; the community runs on Discord and the community platform.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Classic "give the buildable thing" (family E). Difference: ShareAlike instead of CC0, hardware instead of software, and a large community that Amélie lacks.

**What Amélie learns.** A gift grows when plans, tools, business-model templates and a community come together. Here too: dispute and administration come with size.

**Stance when in contact: Community channels only.** Via FAQ and community only. The foundation explicitly gives no individual feedback on machine building, product design, business or personal ideas. Email only if the question fits neither FAQ nor community.

**Contact routes**

- [hello@preciousplastic.com](mailto:hello@preciousplastic.com): General (page read)
- <https://www.preciousplastic.com/contact>: Contact page with rules (page read)
- <https://community.preciousplastic.com>: Community and Discord (page read)

### Open Source Ecology (OSE)

**Status:** active · **Place:** Missouri, USA / weltweit · **Since:** 2003

> Open blueprints for 50 machines that let small communities supply themselves.

**What they do.** Marcin Jakubowski founded OSE in 2003 after his doctorate at the University of Wisconsin because research felt "too closed off from the world’s problems". The core is the Global Village Construction Set (GVCS): 50 industrial machines from tractor to brick press as an "open technological platform". By 2018 it was 33 per cent complete. Kickstarter 2011 raised $63,573, Shuttleworth Fellowship 2012 to 2014, TIME listed the "Civilization Starter Kit" among 2012 inventions. In 2016 a group of 50 built the "Seed Eco-Home" of 1,400 sq ft in five days, material cost about $30,000, about $50,000 by 2022. OSE Germany operates independently; the focus shifted to affordable housing.

**Model, licence, scale.** Wiki-based documentation, forum, IRC. The licence details were not read here. The site currently calls itself "not media-ready" (infrastructure being rebuilt).

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Same "give the buildable thing" stance, but with a very large ambition (50 machines) and slow completion. Amélie stays small and delivers one-pagers.

**What Amélie learns.** An over-large catalogue stays unfinished for years (33 per cent after 15 years). Amélie’s tins are deliberately small and individually deliverable.

**Stance when in contact: Community channels only.** Via wiki and forum, or the general address. Leadership has its own address, but a greeting there is unnecessary for Amélie.

**Contact routes**

- [info@opensourceecology.org](mailto:info@opensourceecology.org): General (page read)
- [director@opensourceecology.org](mailto:director@opensourceecology.org): Leadership (founder and CEO) (page read)
- <https://www.opensourceecology.org/contact/>: Contact page (social, IRC, conferences) (page read)

## Idea gifters and idea banks

*Who drops ideas without a brief. Finding: raw lists stay unread, delivery to named people is missing.*

### open-source-ideas (GitHub)

**Status:** active · **Place:** GitHub · **Since:** nicht ermittelt

> Anyone with an OSS idea but no time posts it as an issue; others build it.

**What they do.** Crowdsourced collection of open-source project ideas. Sharers file an issue with effort (little, medium, much), difficulty (beginner to advanced) and categories (web, AI/ML, mobile, IoT, developer tools). Seekers filter the issues; progress is in the comments, finished projects enter the "Hall of Fame". Figures: 6.8k stars, 231 forks, 276 open issues, 11 projects in the hall of fame, over 200 active ideas. Rule set: Contributor Covenant.

**Model, licence, scale.** Open GitHub organisation, moderated by the community. The ideas have no recipient and no skeleton.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** The direct parallel that best shows what Amélie does differently: there the idea sits in the room, here a named person with a mandate gets the idea plus a runnable skeleton.

**What Amélie learns.** 11 built projects against over 200 ideas is the rate without addressing. Use it as a benchmark for Amélie’s delivery rate.

**Stance when in contact: Show, do not ask.** An issue with an idea Amélie cannot deliver itself (one-pager plus link) is the natural route; nothing more.

**Contact routes**

- <https://github.com/open-source-ideas/open-source-ideas>: Repository (submit an idea as an issue) (page read)
- <https://open-source-ideas.github.io/>: Website (snippet only, verify)

### captn3m0/ideas

**Status:** active · **Place:** GitHub · **Since:** nicht ermittelt

> Personal idea list under CC BY 4.0; whoever builds something from it gets a postcard.

## Blueprint commons

*Open plans that actually get built: the executable gift.*

### WikiHouse

**Status:** active · **Place:** London, UK · **Since:** 2011

> Open CNC house systems: plywood parts that snap together without formal training.

**What they do.** Started in summer 2011 by Alastair Parvin and Nick Ierodiaconou of the London studio 00 with James Arthur, Tav and Steve Fisher, presented at the Gwangju Design Biennale in South Korea. You download design files, adapt them in SketchUp, cut plywood on a CNC router and fit the parts together with wedges and pegs; assembly in under a day. TEDGlobal prize 2012, then WikiHouseRio in Brazil’s favelas; by 2015 prototypes in several countries, with variations such as FOUNDhouse and WikiSHED. Today there is a foundation, the GitHub project "Skylark", a forum, a newsletter and approved manufacturers.

**Model, licence, scale.** Creative Commons ShareAlike (not CC0). The brand name is reserved for approved manufacturers and partners. Test data (structural, environmental, safety) is contributed by organisations.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Blueprint gift with a community, but licence and trade mark against enclosure. Amélie relies on CC0 and defensive publication instead of a mark.

**What Amélie learns.** Between open plans and a real house lie approval, structural engineering and manufacturers. For tins with a standards link too: the route from plan to use needs partners.

**Stance when in contact: Community channels only.** Forum or contact page. The address hello@wikihouse.cc comes from search snippets only, the contact page was read.

### L’Atelier Paysan

**Status:** active · **Place:** Frankreich · **Since:** 2009

> Cooperative in which farmers design and build their own tools.

**What they do.** Founded in 2009 in the south of France from the initiative of a farmer and a technician who opposed the appropriation of farm technology by corporations. Today a collective of small-scale farmers, employees and agricultural development organisations organised as a cooperative (SCIC). Once a design is agreed by consensus, the cooperative publishes it as an open plan and spreads it through workshops and courses: welding, woodwork, mechanics, farm electricity, from open work days to intensive courses. Online there is a tool library of validated designs, technical drawings and tutorials in French and English.

**Model, licence, scale.** All plans under Creative Commons licences. Funding from courses, cooperative shares and grants (details not read).

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** The gift as craft: not an idea but plan plus course. Difference: hardware, cooperative, French-speaking, a fixed audience (organic farming).

**What Amélie learns.** A fixed circle of recipients with a shared need (expensive, ill-fitting machines) makes the gift connectable. Amélie’s rule 2 (real person, concrete mandate) is the same principle.

**Stance when in contact: Community channels only.** French-speaking. Via the contact page or the animation team; do not use the personal addresses from search snippets without cause.

### Farm Hack

## Legal tools

*How a gift stays a gift: defensive publication, DOI, hardware openness.*

### Technical Disclosure Commons (TDCommons)

**Status:** active · **Place:** online · **Since:** ca. 2015 (Datum nicht bestätigt)

> Free platform for defensive publications: prior art against enclosure.

**What they do.** A repository for defensive publications. Publishing a technical description makes it dated and findable for patent examiners so others can no longer patent it. The whole collection can be indexed by search engines, including Google Patents. It is used mostly by companies that want to keep side inventions free. A snippet cites over 1,500 publications (date unknown).

**Model, licence, scale.** Free, account required, via "Submit a Defensive Publication"; submissions without required revisions usually post within 72 hours. Operator: the FAQ says the site is operated by bepress at the request of Google, another page names Elsevier through the Digital Commons platform. The landscape document’s claim that it is run at Santa Clara University School of Law could not be confirmed here and should be corrected or sourced.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Not kin in spirit but the tool that keeps Amélie’s gifts given. The landscape document: nobody in the scene uses it.

**What Amélie learns.** Plan a defensive publication for every tin where enclosure is realistic (hardware-adjacent, measurement, sensing). Costs nothing, takes an afternoon.

**Stance when in contact: Use as a tool.** Use, do not contact. For publication questions use the contact page.

**Contact routes**

- <https://www.tdcommons.org/contact.html>: Contact page (page read)
- <https://www.tdcommons.org/faq.html>: FAQ and author FAQ (page read)

*Evidence: page read, checked 2026-10-01.*

### Zenodo

**Status:** active · **Place:** CERN / OpenAIRE · **Since:** nicht ermittelt

> Open repository with DOI: the second route to defensive publication.

**What they do.** Run by CERN and OpenAIRE, also EU-funded, built on InvenioRDM. Every upload gets a DOI, with links to ORCID and GitHub. Several authors already use Zenodo for prior-art publications with an explicit CC0 dedication.

**Model, licence, scale.** The default licence is CC BY 4.0, CC0 must be chosen explicitly (snippet). Amélie’s roadmap plans automatic DOI minting via Zenodo and TDCommons.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** A tool, not kin. Especially fitting because CERN itself put the web software into the public domain in 1993.

**What Amélie learns.** A DOI makes tins citable and dated, free of charge. Complements TDCommons, where patent examiners look.

**Stance when in contact: Use as a tool.** Use. Support via the help page.

**Contact routes**

- <https://zenodo.org/support>: Support (page read)
- <https://help.zenodo.org/>: Help and documentation (page read)

*Evidence: page read, checked 2026-10-01.*

### Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA)

**Status:** active · **Place:** USA · **Since:** 2012

> Definition and certification for open hardware, over 3,400 certified projects.

**What they do.** Nonprofit (501c3), founded in 2012 by Alicia Gibb among others. It maintains the Open Hardware Definition ("design made publicly available so anyone can study, modify, distribute, make and sell it") and a certification programme that doubles as a catalogue. The site shows 3,430 certified projects.

**Model, licence, scale.** Certification, resources, events, membership. OSHWA has no defensive-publication service in its own material, but third parties point out that open hardware remains patentable without prior art.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Relevant only for tins with a hardware part. Its catalogue of certified projects is an occupancy test for hardware ideas.

**What Amélie learns.** Open hardware needs a definition and a mark, otherwise "open" is not verifiable. Amélie’s CC0 pledge has the same verification problem.

**Stance when in contact: Use as a tool.** Use (catalogue, definition). Contact only for certification questions.

**Contact routes**

- <https://www.oshwa.org/>: Website (page read)
- <https://oshwa.org/definition/>: Open Hardware Definition (snippet only, verify)

*Evidence: page read, checked 2026-10-01.*

## Civic-tech neighbours

*Places where wishes, builders and directories live.*

### Wikimedia Community Wishlist

**Status:** active · **Place:** Wikimedia Foundation · **Since:** 2015

> The community wishes, the foundation builds: a structured pipeline from wish to delivery.

**What they do.** In November 2015 the Community Tech team ran the first cross-project wishlist survey: 634 participants proposed, discussed and voted on 107 ideas. From 2015 to 2020, 30 of the top-ten proposals were completed, 12 declined and 3 partially fulfilled. Since 2024 a continuous intake system. The 2026/27 cycle: submit wishes until 8 November 2026, triage 9 to 20 November, voting 8 to 24 January 2027, implementation from March 2027. Britta Gustafson (Dreamyshade) becomes lead programme manager on 20 October 2026.

**Model, licence, scale.** A paid organisation builds what the community wishes by majority. No money to the wishers, but development work.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** The one example where wishes reach a named builder with a mandate. Amélie’s pattern (wish to a named person) in institutional form, but only for Wikimedia technology.

**What Amélie learns.** Delivery works when wish and build team sit in the same organisation. Rate 2015 to 2020: 30 of 45 decided top-ten wishes delivered.

**Stance when in contact: Show, do not ask.** Only if a tin has a Wikimedia link (tools for editors, Commons, Wikidata). Then submit a wish by 8 November 2026, otherwise not.

**Contact routes**

- <https://meta.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=Special:WishlistIntake&returnto=Community_Wishlist>: Submit a wish (page read)
- <https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Community_Wishlist>: Overview (page read)

*Evidence: page read, checked 2026-10-01.*

### OK Lab Berlin (Code for Germany)

**Status:** active · **Place:** Berlin · **Since:** 2014 (Code for Germany)

> Civic-tech community in Berlin with about 30 active members, meeting on the second Monday of each month.

**What they do.** OK Lab Berlin is the Berlin group of Code for Germany, the national programme of Open Knowledge Foundation Germany (founded 2011, based in Berlin), which started in February 2014 with Open Knowledge Labs in eight cities. About 30 people work in groups on open-data and civic-tech projects, such as "Wir zählen" (making traffic counts visible) and a street-tree API. Meetings: every second Monday of the month at Wikibär, Köpenicker Straße 45.

**Model, licence, scale.** Volunteer group, open meetings, GitHub organisation codeforberlin, Mastodon and Meetup.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** Not kin in the narrow sense, but the local place where Amélie’s tins with an administration or data link meet people who could build them.

**What Amélie learns.** The Prototype Fund is also run by Open Knowledge Foundation Germany; this milieu is therefore also the funding route (see funding compass).

**Stance when in contact: Show, do not ask.** Go to a meeting and show something, ask for nothing. Fitting: tins with a Berlin link (street-name checker, noise map).

### Civic Tech Field Guide

**Status:** active · **Place:** weltweit, gehostet bei Superbloom · **Since:** 2016

> Worldwide directory of civic-tech projects, with its own "graveyard" of failed projects.

**What they do.** Conceived in early 2016 by Micah Sifry (Civic Hall), Matt Stempeck (then Microsoft) and Erin Simpson as an open spreadsheet; in 2018 Stempeck built it into a directory under Civic Hall, supported by the Knight Foundation, Luminate and the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation. Today a project of Superbloom, also supported by Sarapis and donations. Projects can be listed or "claimed", there are volunteers and curators. Notably: a "graveyard" with the text "Learning from the civic tech graveyard".

**What Amélie learns.** Search the directory before any civic-tech idea round. Listing Amélie as a project would be a greeting without mail traffic.

### Up For Grabs

**Status:** active · **Place:** GitHub Pages · **Since:** nicht ermittelt

> Connects contributors with curated, self-contained starter tasks in open-source projects.

**What they do.** A platform where projects list themselves with a label (e.g. "up-for-grabs") when their issues are well described, self-contained and doable in a few evenings. Maintained by dahlbyk, shiftkey, jrusbatch and ritwik12. Projects add themselves by pull request to the repository `up-for-grabs/up-for-grabs.net`.

**Model, licence, scale.** Open GitHub Pages project, listing by pull request.

**Why a sister, where Amélie differs.** The "few evenings of work" format matches ticket 01 of a tin. Up For Grabs is where a ticket becomes individually findable.

**What Amélie learns.** Good tickets are described, self-contained and small. That is also Amélie’s quality bar for ticket 01.

**Stance when in contact: Use as a tool.** Use as a bridge for ticket 01: list a code repo with the label. No contact needed.
